title: The Smartest Budget SUV With A Toyota Badge Will Make You Forget About The Honda HR-V - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update Some would consider the Honda HR-V to be the gold standard in affordable, versatile family SUVs. It starts at just $26,600, it seats five, and, while a 158-hp powertrain might not make it a powerhouse, it's more than enough for a daily driver. But, with all due respect for Honda, we would argue that the Toyota Corolla Cross is actually the better SUV in this price range, beating the CR-V in almost every category that matters. What are we looking for in a family-sized budget-friendly SUV? Well, a nice low price, for starters. Beyond that, a comfortable ride, excellent safety ratings, and a reliable powertrain are all must-haves. So, how do the 2027 HR-V and the 2026 Corolla Cross stack up in these areas? Our Quality & Reliability ratings come from JD Power, while our overall crash test ratings come from the NHTSA. These numbers show the Corolla Cross taking a lead by matching the HR-V for safety and reliability, while producing more power, and selling for $1,265 less than the Honda. The HR-V does beat the Corolla Cross when it comes to IIHS ratings. The Honda holds a Top Safety Pick+ award for the current model year, while the Corolla Cross earns a Top Safety Pick, the silver medal to Honda's gold, essentially. Both earned top honors in the front crash prevention: pedestrian category, so this may be splitting hairs. Honda offers a bit more space in most dimensions. The Corolla Cross gives you an extra inch of leg room up front, but when it comes to the back row, the HR-V is a bit roomier. Roomy might be a stretch when talking about either of these subcompact crossovers, but the HR-V does provide an extra inch of breathing room here and there. For a car to be affordable demands not just that the sticker price is nice and low, but that the cost of ownership is reasonable, as well. When we compare these two SUVs head to head, the Honda HR-V ultimately pulls ahead, but by a very slim margin. We went with CarEdge for our annual maintenance and insurance estimates, while FuelEconomy.gov provides us with our fuel expenses comparison. For insurance, CarEdge assumes full coverage for a 40-year-old driver with good credit and a clean record. Fuel expenses assume 15,000 annual miles, split 45/55 between highway and city driving. The HR-V is a bit cheaper to keep than the Corolla Cross, by a difference of $179. But, the Corolla Cross is $1,265 cheaper off the lot, so it would take seven years to make up the difference in ownership expenses. Comparing the Corolla Cross to some of the leading small SUVs, here's what we turn up. Our argument isn't so much that the Corolla Cross is the dominant winner in every single category. You can easily find cheaper, more powerful cars than the Corolla Cross. But, the Corolla Cross is a remarkably well-rounded, capable SUV at a very low price. We could just as easily make an argument for the Crosstrek. If you can afford the price difference, the Crosstrek does outperform the Corolla Cross in more areas than not, but it's $1,660 more expensive, and, being all-wheel-drive exclusive, will cost you around $2,100 a year in fuel expenses, compared to $1,900 for the Corolla Cross. The Toyota Corolla Cross has been around since the 2022 model year, and you would think that that would be long enough for it to have lost its first chunk of resale value. Well, think again. A 2022 Corolla Cross L 2WD is currently trending at $21,998 from an MSRP of $22,445. If you're waiting for Toyota values to take a dive, you're going to be waiting a long time. CarEdge estimates a Toyota typically loses around 35% of its value after five years on the market, ranking it among the best brands overall for resale value. The Corolla Cross is estimated to lose just 30% of its value after five years on the road, making it a slow depreciator even for a Toyota. Checking the used auto market, we find the following models for sale. Note that these listings are just to give you an example of what's out there. There's no telling what will be available when you're ready to shop around. More importantly, we'd like to know how someone put 43,442 miles on a Corolla Cross in just a year or two. But seriously, our point is that these numbers prove that it's kind of not worth buying a used model just yet. For perspective, let's refresh ourselves on the MSRPs for a new Corolla Cross. If you can get a good deal on a used Corolla Cross, a used Toyota will outlast most new models. But, you'll be saving so little money on a low-mileage used Corolla Cross that it's not really worth the hassle. The only listings that are selling for significantly less than new models are already nearing six digits on the odometer. We find the Corolla Cross to be very easy to recommend to just about anyone in the market for a daily driver. If you need something a little more rugged for broken roads and rural unpaved driveways, we'll recommend a Crosstrek. If you need something dirt cheap, the Chevy Trax is remarkably affordable. If you want something that does a lil' of this and a lil' of that, the Corolla Cross is it. Reliable, affordable, capable, and safe. It's not a specialty car by any stretch of the imagination. To put it one way, you could say that it's excellent at a few things, like dependability and, of course, affordability, and it's not bad at anything. To put it another way, you could call it the vanilla ice cream of the small SUV segment, but that's not always a bad thing. Think about it, when you're hosting a party for the whole family, what flavor are you going with? Sources: Honda, Toyota, Mazda, Chevrolet, Subaru, NHTSA, IIHS, CarEdge, FuelEconomy.gov. title: Would you pay $73,000 for a 14-year-old Cadillac CTS-V Wagon? Well, someone just did! - autoevolution
content:
Depreciation is a killer for new cars. On average, a new car loses 20% of its value within the first year, with about 10% vanishing the moment you drive it off the dealership lot. This 2012 Cadillac CTS-V Wagon, however, went in the opposite direction. Originally driven off the lot for $69,940, it just sold for $73,000. Wagons are a dying breed. However, there are people out there who are wagon diehards and would do anything for a brutal, manual-transmission long roof. This 2012 Cadillac CTS-V Wagon seems to check those boxes. Finished in Mocha Steel Metallic over a Light Titanium interior, the wagon rides on 19-inch multi-spoke wheels, wrapped in tires date-coded 2017 and 2018, respectively, which need to be replaced ASAP by the new owner. Let’s do numbers first. So the original owner paid $69,940 to drive this car off the showroom floor. Fourteen years, a few owners, and 43,272 miles (69,640 kilometers) later, it found a new home. Listed on Cars and Bids, the car stole the show, but bidding failed to reach the reserve, so it was sold afterward for $73,000. That’s a solid $3,000 over the sticker price from 14 years ago. Those make it flash from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 4.0 secods nd max at 185 mph when fitted with the manual transmission, like this car is. The six-speed gearbox puts the power down through the rear wheels. A limited-slip differential is part of the plan. With all those specs and the family-oriented body style, every dad out there can be sure kids will never be late to school. Brembo brakes provide the stopping power when the dad pulls up to school, while the Magnetic Ride Control filters the road imperfections and reduces body roll for more comfort on board. In the meantime, mom and dad sit in heated Recaro seats. The UltraView sunroof lets the light of a sunny day in, the rearview camera makes the Caddy easier to maneuver when parking, and the Bose sound system provides the soundtrack when those on board have had enough of the V8 orchestra. At over 43,000 miles, the wagon is far from perfect: some chips show up on the front end, while the driver’s seat displays the usual signs of wear. However, those seem to be the only issues that the buyer will have to deal with. They also got two keys, the owner's manual, and the window sticker. The Carfax report shows a clean past with no accidents or mileage discrepancies and registrations in Southern states since new. Elena started off as a sports reporter and five years later switched to automotive. How does that happen? Lots of writing, testdrives, traveling, off-road driving courses, track driving courses, defensive driving courses and diplomas. The diplomas might be "useless", but the knowledge she gained is priceless.

title: Aston Villa v Arsenal: How the players rated in the Gunners' narrow victory - BBC
content: Bukayo Saka's goal gave Arsenal a 1-0 victory at Aston Villa. Here's how BBC Sport rated the players, and how you rated them. Zion Suzuki: A debut for the £30m goalkeeper from Parma who had no chance with the opening goal. Misjudged his first corner but his distribution caught the eye and will be useful this season. 7 Matty Cash: His usual solid display and got the better of Christos Tzolis, who was replaced at the break. 6 Pau Torres: Helped keep Arsenal at bay until they broke the deadlock in the second half. 6 Victor Lindelof: The Sweden international diligently tried to keep Arsenal in check. Has not let Villa down since arriving on a free transfer. 6 Ian Maatsen: With new signing Matteo Ruggeri on the bench, he has competition and had his hands full with Bukayo Saka, and was beaten to the ball for the goal. 6 Boubacar Kamara: The midfielder is so crucial to how Villa play and he offered an important shield to frustrate the Gunners until Saka's opener. 7 Ross Barkley: The former Everton youngster has been given a second chance at Villa as they rebuild and tried to keep the hosts flowing. 6 John McGinn: The skipper drilled over and was his usual energetic self as Villa tried to unsettle Arsenal and did not drop his energy levels. 6 Emi Buendia: The Argentina international hit the bar early and was a good creative outlet for the hosts but could not find the killer touch. 6 George Hemmings: Villa rate the 19-year-old highly and he showed no fear against the champions. He threatened in the first half, especially with one low cross. 7 Nicolas Jackson: The £65m record signing will take time as he replaces Ollie Watkins but showed flashes of what he can bring. 6 Tammy Abraham (on 71, Jackson): Included despite Ipswich trying to take him on loan, but could not find a leveller. 6 Alysson (on 71, Hemmings):  Winger looked lively in second-half cameo. 6 Alejandro Garnacho (on 78, Barkley): Could not provide late magic. 5 Aaron Wan-Bissaka (on 78, Cash): Debut appearance came late on. 5 Subs not used: Bizot, Bogarde, Lynch, Mings, Ruggeri Bukayo Saka scored in the second half to give Arsenal the lead David Raya: A reliable display from Raya. A good range of passing. 6 Ben White: He didn't produce his usual overlapping runs as much but helped the Arsenal back four keep a clean sheet. 6 Cristhian Mosquera: The 22-year-old produced a solid performance next to the more experienced Gabriel. Had to come off with an injury in the second half. 6 Gabriel Magalhaes: A chance early on from an Arsenal corner which he headed over. The Brazilian led the Arsenal back four as they picked up three points. 7 Riccardo Calafiori: Picked up his usual adventurous positions when Arsenal were going forward and provided the assist for Saka's goal. 8 Declan Rice: Assured in the middle of the pitch and covered a lot of ground. Some important interceptions and threatening set-pieces too. 6 Myles Lewis-Skelly: Continued his excellent start-of-season form. Comfortable when under pressure and played with a lot of responsibility. 7 Martin Odegaard: A couple of nice passes in the first half but not enough impact going forward. Went close with a free-kick in the second half. 6 Bukayo Saka: The winger scored the vital goal for Arsenal. The Gunners were not at their best going forward but most of the good moments involved Saka. 8 Christos Tzolis: A disappointing night for the winger who worked hard but lacked quality when going forward. Taken off at half-time. 4 Kai Havertz: It was a quiet night for Havertz but the forward still provided a focal point and held the ball up. 6 Eberechi Eze (on 46, Tzolis): Introduced at half-time and played a big part in Saka's goal. 7 Merino (on 71, Odegaard): Added bite into the Arsenal midfield. 6 Bruno Guimaraes (on 71, Lewis-Skelly): On for his Arsenal Premier League debut. 6 Ezri Konsa (on 78, Mosquera): Made first appearance for his new club. 6 Martin Zubimendi (on 85, Rice): Came on for Rice as Arsenal looked to see out the game. 5 After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: 2026 Cadillac CT5 V-Series Blackwing Review: All Hail The King - Yahoo Autos
content: Pour one out for a legend: 2026 marks the spectacular Cadillac CT5 V-Series Blackwing's final year of production as GM phases out the platform to replace both the CT4 and CT5 with one vehicle. Let us not dwell on the loss; the fact that the Blackwing exists and is so incredible to experience, interact with, and drive is a beacon of fire and lightning and brutalist thunder amidst a world of gray. No car in its class can compare to the CT5-V Blackwing when it comes to inspiring you to have a good time on open or twisty roads alike, and it's a car that will stand as a legend for eras to come. Among a species that is becoming increasingly endangered, Cadillac's CT5 V-Series Blackwing gets better with every iteration. The Precision Package makes the Blackwing a world-class super-sedan and perhaps the best-driving four-door production car on the planet. The chassis, steering, cornering, acceleration, endless power, braking, and overall amazing way of communicating to the driver is almost otherworldly, especially when considering the segment's other occupants. The Blackwing will go down as one of the best sports/super-sedans of all time, and every fragment of that is warranted. It's a forever car if there ever was one. Not much changed for 2026, but there were changes last year. The CT5 received an interior update for 2025, the majority of which entails a 33-inch LED color touchscreen. Outside, the car got a redesigned grille and front fascia, and new colors. 2026 saw only the addition of safety equipment, plus Performance Data Recorder (PDR) and Blind Zone Steering Assist are now standard. Despite its unhinged driving manners when you let the Blackwing do its thing, the car's exterior design is really rather restrained. The test car's Carbon Fiber 1 and Carbon Fiber 2 packages don't do that notion any favors, though. The car's otherwise fairly straightforward and angular bodywork is more luxury car than performance. The big exhaust tips and vents are really the only telltale signs on a base Blackwing that a beast is lying under the hood. Frankly, that's how we like our performance sedans: Those who know know, but you can otherwise fly under the radar. Save the flaunt and flash for the sports cars; the best sport and super-sedans only show what they're capable of when you let them loose. Oh glory, oh lordy, oh heavenly spectacularness, what a fun time the supercharged 6.2-liter LT4 V8 is. The thumping engine pumps out 668 horsepower and 659 lb-ft of torque, available for your choosing paired to a Tremec TR6060 six-speed manual or 10-speed Hydra-Matic 10L90 automatic gearbox. The car weighs around 4,100 pounds in either guise, so the power-to-weight doesn't match that of true featherweights, but at least this car is still hardly over the two-ton mark. It's not light per se, but it's certainly light for the class, and the LT4 revels in that. Goddamn, this car is rowdy. In a world where Corvettes pump out 1,000+ horsepower from the factory, the Blackwing's paltry 668 horsepower still feels absolutely mega by day-to-day standards. Forget what the internet says; anywhere you go in this car, you're the big daddy. Left foot hard on the brake, right foot hard on the gas, prepare your body and soul, then dump the brake away and let the demon under the hood run free. Rear-wheel-drive is absolutely no match for this much power, even despite the Michelins doing their damndest to keep the car accelerating forward. Needless to say, you can incinerate the rear tires at the lightest prod of your foot with traction control off, and even with every system fully engaged it's easy to break traction at near-highway speeds when there's water on the roadways. It's good-née great-fun, the kind of involving excitement that other cars just don't tout. You have to drive the Blackwing slightly scared of it, or it will bite you. And that's a huge amount of the Blackwing's charm. In a world littered with EVs and all-wheel-drive cars that can easily out-accelerate the Blackwing, its relatively old-school small-block V8 and Eaton blower bring you immediate response from the accelerator and what feels like a look back into the past. When so many cars are turbocharged, and there's that minute gap between your right foot and the reaction of the engine, the LT4 really shines bright. It feels like an old racing engine compared to other modern motors. Speaking of yesteryear, about that gas mileage… Ha. Haha. Hahahaha. Good one. Oh, and speaking of "one," I often saw gas mileage in the single-digit range during my week of testing this Blackwing (and the others I've spent time with, too). You really gotta pay to play with this engine under your right foot. Somehow, though, the press car showed a 17 MPG tally for the 1000-mile Trip A meter, but there must have been a lot of highway involved before my loan. The EPA rates the gas mileage at 13 city, 20 highway, 15 combined, and we all know their test is fairly lenient. Expect sub-15 if you own this car, even babying it. A few hard pulls and you can literally watch the fuel gauge drop before your eyes. The aforementioned comparatively light weight also pays huge dividends in the handling and cornering departments. The controls are both delicate and hefty, the chassis alive and composed. You are in control of your own driving fate in the Blackwing; sure, there's (very competent and complex) computers on board, but they don't do much more than help you not crash coming out of a corner or when launching hard off the line. The Blackwing just lets you drive, and rewards you beautifully regardless of how hard you're pushing. Drivability on the Blackwing spectrum is truly phenomenal, especially considering how much performance is on tap. It's such an easy car to drive whether around town or on the highway that if it wasn't for the LT4's burble and how easy the motor makes acceleration from any speed, you can easily forget just how potent it is. But one slip or deliberate prod of the right foot and you can suddenly see extra-legal speeds or go very sideways within seconds, so you have to respect the car a bit more than in comparable vehicles that have all-wheel-drive. Even so, if you want to daily drive the Blackwing and pretend it's a point-to-point Prius-esque people carrier, it's happy to oblige (save for that gas mileage aspect; yikes). Given what the suspension is tasked with managing when the engine is at full chat, Blackwing's ride quality is very respectable. You definitely know this car is tuned for performance every time you go over a bump, but kudos to the chassis engineers for putting together underpinnings that are nothing short of amazing. Comfort is high, though there isn't a ton of room in the back seat and the roofline makes loading children and car seats in and out a bit of a harder task than is ideal. It's much less useful as far as the family use case goes compared to the M5 Touring, or RS6 Avant for that matter, but it's only slightly less back seat-friendly than the M5 sedan. Remember when there was a CTS-V Wagon, though? Oh how we long for a Blackwing Wagon… Up front, the driver and person riding shotgun will be more than pleased with the accommodations; heated, ventilated, and massaging seats certainly help, and there's enough space to get comfy when on a long haul. You can't forget that the Blackwing is based on what is already a luxury car, so that it rides well and has good baseline levels of comfort isn't a shock. Cadillac hasn't been known for its interior style in, well, eons. That's not any different here in the Blackwing, as the car is very function-forward as it puts design in the proverbial passenger seat. That's not something we find issue with, though it does bring down the dealer showroom "wow factor" some. Quality is decent though, with our one qualm in the style-and-quality realm being GM's choice of switchgear. There are a lot of sub-$50k car buttons and knobs in there, all of which are hard to palate at the Blackwing's $100k base and $150k as-tested prices, but that's like criticizing the best BBQ you've ever eaten for the restaurant having thin napkins. You're not buying the car for its buttons, so maybe we're nitpicking for no reason. This generation of Cadillac (and General Motors) infotainment is very good. It brings everything you want front and center in the dashboard, and the way the screen angles towards the driver in the case of the updated CT5 interior architecture makes toggling through HVAC, media, or performance-related menus and settings incredibly easy, even when on the move. The whole infotainment is truthfully really pleasant to use: It's fast to respond, intuitive, and it avoids being overwhelming even despite the 33-inch screen effectively dominating the dashboard and interior as a whole. This iteration of GM infotainment even has wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, which GM foolishly removed from its next round of infotainment for reasons only their finance department can justify. Our only complaint is you have to use a cheap-feeling dial to control it when not using the touchscreen functionality, but otherwise it doesn't leave us asking for anything more. SuperCruise, too, surpasses what you expect given the confines of modern pricing structures. We have a hard time loving hands-free driving aids (ADAS) as hardcore driving enthusiasts, yet SuperCruise continues to impress. Do dollars and sense really matter here? When the prospective buyer wants a car that meshes high-power Corvette thrills, excitement, and thrust with Cadillac luxury, refinement, and performance? And has the money to pay for it all? Dollars matter more than emotion for some, but that's not the case for a Blackwing buyer. We mere mortals-those like yours truly and most other journalists reviewing Blackwings-have to juggle things that most six-digit Cadillac buyers don't often consider. Still, you have to be a special kind of buyer to seek out the CT5 V-Series Blackwing. It's not exactly your grandma's Caddy, and the way you can option and spec this car above and beyond its core sure is something. Emotion overrides financial sense, through and through. For the sake of looking at the money aspect, the 2026 Cadillac CT5 V-Series Blackwing starts with a $98,900 base price (before Destination), which is probably the best way for most people to buy. Not that anyone needs 668 horsepower in the first place, but everything else that can be added really just goes above and beyond and makes only incremental differences as far as the on-road and daily-driving Blackwing experience goes. Track drivers, the few of them, might feel differently though, so GM has options on tap for that glorious bunch. The big ticket item in this test car's spec is the $18,000 Precision Package which adds, per Cadillac: Increased spring rates, larger front stabilizer bar and revised suspension bushings New front steering knuckles and rear suspension toe links which allow for more aggressive wheel alignment for track usage Recalibrated subsystems: MagneRide dampers, steering, chassis controls and Electronic Limited Slip Differential (eLSD) Whether you want any of that on top of an already-incredible vehicle is not for us to discuss, but I've said it before and will say it again: $18k buys a lot of tire, gas, and track day insurance. Yet for argument's sake, $18k probably doesn't mean much to someone who can afford a Blackwing, and the cost of the package will probably return at least half of the deal on the back end should someone (for some ungodly reason) go to sell the car. Buyers probably also don't need the $13k worth of carbon fiber draped around this car, and the stick shift would save you $3,675. Super Cruise is solid-- we'd keep that-- but $107k buys an otherwise pretty perfect CT5 Blackwing. No doubt that's still a ton of money. It's a relative value proposition compared to an M5 or even the way this test car was optioned (which can run up to right under $160k with the Deep Ocean package and shipping via an enclosed carrier; GM is really milking this car's final year). Even the Blackwing we tested last year was optioned similarly and "only" cost $138k, so there's certainly some price creep, and the last M5 I tested was $141k. The four-door M5's sedan counterpart starts at $123k and can be optioned to almost $150k, while Porsche's closest offering (the Panamera GTS) is going to be $50k more if you so much as look at the build sheet the wrong way. Points to the Blackwing so long as you keep the add-ons in check. Twenty-two years ago, Cadillac debuted the CTS-V to take on the BMW M5, and the legacy that led to the modern Blackwing is dotted with attempts to match Corvette performance with Cadillac refinement on a budget that has its successes and failures. Versus an ebb-and-flow of rivals, we come to the back half of 2026 and find it's only the Blackwing among its immediate competitors that still feels like a car with lineage and tactical, feel-it-in-your-hands-and-soul ties to its predecessors. Every ounce of that is for the better, and the Blackwing is the best-driving, most exciting gas-powered sedan on sale today. Let us wax poetic: It doesn't get better than this. The 2026 Cadillac CT5 V-Series Blackwing is the only pure, raw (yet comfortable) ultra-high-performance sedan left on the market. Everything else (wagon competitors included) coddles to the point of detriment as far as driving goes, and the Blackwing simply makes every outing an experience or adventure. Though the all-wheel-drive and hybridized competition is quicker off the line and generally more efficient, the CT5-V Blackwing is the easy "forever car" pick of the litter thanks to how it makes you feel when behind the wheel. This car's driving experience just doesn't exist anywhere else in the class, and it's a sad thing for us enthusiasts to acknowledge this year is the last time the modern Blackwing will be on sale. It's one for the ages, and we will miss it dearly. (The manufacturer provided insurance and a tank of fuel for this loan, and big thanks as always to the team at FMI for arranging and coordinating logistics. - RB) Settles down beautifully when not being hammered on No wagon version (lest we further lament the loss of the CTS-V Wagon) Handling, cornering, steering, braking, acceleration, etc - Everything related to how it drives Drives exotic but doesn't feel it - switchgear and the likes feel more economy-car grade

title: Norway's Queen Mette-Marit joins procession to bring late King Harald V's coffin to royal chapel - AP News
content: Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All Rights Reserved. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All Rights Reserved. The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title. King Harald V of Norway and his wife Sonja leave the Notre Dame cathedral after attending at the funeral of the Grand Duke Jean of Luxembourg, in Luxembourg, on May 4, 2019. (AP Photo/Francisco Seco, File) Norway’s King Harald V’s coffin is placed in the Palace Chapel in Oslo, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. (Cornelius Poppe/Pool Photo via AP) Norway’s Queen Mette-Mari, Queen Sonja, Princess Märtha Louise and King Haakon come out to the Palace Square to greet the people and look at the sea of flowers and greetings that mourners have laid down four days after the death of King Harald V, in Oslo Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. (Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix via AP) Norway’s King Harald V’s coffin is moved by King Harald’s family and court staff from the Red Salon to the Palace Chapel in Oslo, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. (Javad Parsa/Pool Photo via AP) King Harald V’s coffin is moved by King Haakon VIII., left, and and Queen Mette-Marit’s son Marius Borg Hoiby, second right, from the Red Salon to the Palace Chapel, in Oslo, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. (Ole Berg-Rusten/Pool Photo via AP) OSLO, Norway (AP) — The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title. Harald passed away Friday at age 89, and his son, the crown prince, immediately became King Haakon VIII. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Haakon, 53, will take the oath to Norway’s constitution on Tuesday. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. Mette-Marit has been largely absent from the public eye in the wake of her lung transplant in June. She was diagnosed in 2018 with pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive disease that damages and scars lung tissue. It can cause serious breathing problems, and there is no known cure. Mette-Marit and Queen Sonja, Harald’s widow, held hands and walked behind the coffin during Monday’s procession. Since Harald’s death, the royal family and the country have been in an official state of mourning. Norwegians and visitors expressed their grief over the weekend by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. The coffin stayed in the palace’s Red Salon over the weekend before traveling to the royal chapel on Monday, where it will remain until the funeral. The public can go to the chapel to pay their respects to the late king beginning Tuesday, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All Rights Reserved. title: King Harald V transferred to the Chapel of the Royal Palace of Oslo - The Royal Watcher
content:
Following the passing of King Harald V at the Rikshospitalet in Oslo, a Cabinet Meeting, and Transfer to the Royal Place of Oslo, the Coffin of the late King Harald V of Norway has been transferred in a Procession through the State Rooms of the Royal Palace of Oslo to the Palace Chapel on August 31st. The Coffin of King Harald has been in the Red Room of the Royal Palace of Oslo since it returned from the Rikshospitalet on August 28th. It has now been moved onto a catafalque and draped in the royal flag. King Harald’s Coffin was carried by his children and grandchildren through the Yellow Salon, the Hall of Mirrors, the Daily Dining Room, the Little Banquet Hall and the Great Banquet Hall to the Palace Chapel, followed by members of the Norwegian Court carrying the late King’s Orders, including the Order of St. Olav, the Order of the Elephant, the Order of the Seraphim, and the Order of the Garter. The bier is carried by King Harald’s children and grandchildren in procession through the Yellow Salon, the Hall of Mirrors, the Daily Dining Room, the Little Banquet Hall and the Great Banquet Hall. Her Majesty the Queen and Queen Sonja are also in the procession, which is led by His Majesty the King’s Chief of Staff. He carries the royal crown on a cushion, and the head of the Royal Secretariat carries the royal sword. Other members of the Court’s leadership carry King Harald’s most important Norwegian, Danish, Swedish and British orders. Employees of the Royal Court form a trellis through the halls of the Palace, joining the procession once King Harald’s bier has passed.In the Great Hall, the adjutant staff takes over the bier and leads it to the Palace Chapel. The bier is placed on a velvet-covered catafalque, and the family’s wreaths and flower hearts will surround the bier. The royal crown and the national sword are placed on the bier. The orders are placed at the foot of the bier. A private memorial service will be held in the Palace Chapel for King Harald’s family, his court and adjutant staff. Afterwards, Queen Sonja (wearing Queen Maud’s Drapers’ Company Brooch) and Princess Märtha Louise joined King Haakon VIII and Queen Mette-Marit to greet the crowd and look at the flowers and tributes that mourners have laid down on Palace Square Queen Sonja, King Haakon VIII, Queen Mette-Marit,  Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, Prince Sverre Magnus, and Princess Märtha Louise followed the Coffin of the late King Harald V of Norway from the Rikshospitalet to the Royal Palace of Oslo. The bier and the royal entourage began their journey from the chapel at the National Hospital, and along the entire route to the Palace, many people had gathered to say goodbye to King Harald. The remains of the late King Harald V of Norway will lie in State at the Royal Palace until the yet to be announced date of the Funeral at Oslo Cathedral before a Burial at the Akershus Fortress. Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra joined King Haakon VIII of Norway for the extraordinary Cabinet Meeting at the Royal Palace of Oslo after the passing of King Harald V of Norway. The Crown Princess will now also attend the weekly Cabinet Meetings and serve as Regent of Norway when required. It is my duty to inform the Council of State that my dear father, His Majesty King Harald V, died today, 28 August 2026 at 06:35, and that in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, I have assumed the government as King of Norway. I will take the name Haakon VIII and will continue the same motto that my father, grandfather and great-grandfather chose: “Everything for Norway.” HM The King thanked the members of the government and the Norwegian people for their support and sympathy for the Royal Family during this time. Yesterday morning at 06:35, His Majesty King Harald V, my father whom I loved so much, died. We are in mourning. At the same time, it gives us comfort and strength that so many people are grieving with us. It has been a powerful and moving experience to see the Palace Square filled with people, flowers, greetings and lights. Thank you very much. My dear father, thank you for being such a good dad to Märtha and me. Warm and safe. You were also a warm and funny grandfather. A loving and caring husband. A generous father-in-law. A brother and uncle who everyone was so happy to be with. You were the head of the family, who, together with my mother, embraced and brought us all together with a natural authority that you may not have been fully aware of yourself. Above all, you were a person who always stood by your values and commitments. You supported and took care of us all. It makes me proud to think about everything you both stood for — and stood up for. I will miss him. I will miss his laugh. His warm way of meeting people and situations. My father always made people around him relax. He was a good listener, especially when dealing with children and young people – for whom he had an extra space in his heart. The big, warm royal hand reached out to everyone, young and old, who needed an extra handshake. He met everyone with respect and generosity – and never discriminated against anyone. He traveled to comfort those affected by the hurricane – dressed in a bubble jacket and rubber boots.
He apologized to the Sami for the injustices committed against them – on behalf of all of us.
He cried with us after we had lost so many on Utøya and in the government quarter.
He brought us together by putting into words who we Norwegians are. I imagine him on the sailboat – with a cap, sunglasses and a resounding laugh. Where he could just be himself, get energy and lots of joy – in competition with other passionate sailors. And the picture of his big smile in the hammock in the Amazon – where he finally fulfilled his boyhood dream of living a few days with the Yanomami people. A dream that arose from a commitment to caring for the world’s animals and nature. Across the country – and around the world – there are thousands of people who today hold the memories they have of meetings with him in high regard. Memories that will live on in people’s hearts and family stories. As king, my father represented Norway and Norwegians with pride and joy. Through visits around the country, at events here at the Palace, and at work for Norway abroad. In the snowdrift at the cross-country stadium.
On the Palace balcony on May 17.
On a state visit to Nelson Mandela. It was also a great strength for him to have my mother, Queen Sonja, as a life partner to share the work with. She contributed to their becoming a strong royal couple who complemented each other well. I know how much she meant to King Harald for standing so firmly in his life’s work. In the life’s work they shared. Today marks 58 years since they got married. Congratulations on your wedding anniversary, dear mother. King Harald accompanied our country through a period of great change. From the time he set foot on Rådhuskaia as an eight-year-old upon his return from World War II – until today – Norway has undergone a great deal of positive development. Today we are a welfare society – where people from different backgrounds live together and figure it out with each other. At the same time, the world is once again more unsafe and unpredictable than it has been during most of King Harald’s reign. Something that also affects us here in this country and has brought a new seriousness to us.Now that my father has passed away, there is a big task ahead of me. He constantly reminded us in the family that everyone must do things their own way. Find their own form. Be themselves. He succeeded his father King Olav – who in turn succeeded his father King Haakon. I am deeply grateful to have my family around me, and for the great support Queen Mette-Marit and our children have for me. I would also like to thank my mother and sister for the strength they share as they themselves grieve the loss of a beloved husband and father. Our family has experienced the importance of standing together to stand strong – both within ourselves and for each other. Even in difficult times. Our unity is a great strength for the work we will do for Norway. After King Harald’s long and eventful reign, it is now up to us to guide each other into a new era. Queen Mette-Marit and I want to be present and listening. The Queen, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and I will always try to understand the life situations of different people. No one knows today what we who live in this country will face together. But what we do know is that we will follow each other through both good and difficult days. We believe in a Norway where we stand securely rooted in our history, in what has shaped us over time.
We believe in our popular government – and in democracy.
We believe in a society built on law and justice – and where everyone is of equal value.
A society where we see and recognize each other’s resources – so that together we can create a Norway where everyone can contribute and feel at home.
We believe in a Norway where there is room for everyone.
We shall feel the strength of our community – and know with ourselves that we are one people. Dear all,
Today I feel a great sense of gratitude towards those who have gone before me. All were kings of their time. They were loved, respected and meant a lot to many. I have learned a lot from them all. Like King Haakon, King Olav and King Harald, I take the election language – “All for Norway”. “Everything for Norway” means fighting for everyone in Norway to have the opportunity to live a free life. It also implies a responsibility to ensure that we as a nation contribute positively to the world. And that means – in the ultimate consequence – being willing to risk everything, including life, for Norway’s freedom and independence. Today we are a family in mourning, and a people in mourning.
We thank King Harald for all he was and all he did – for Norway, – for everyone in our country. With God’s help and the support of the people, I look forward to the great task that lies ahead. title: Is Cannondale's Flying V a Waste of Carbon Fiber? Used To Bring Home the Literal Bacon for $6,500 - autoevolution
content:
Often, carbon fiber bicycles are designed for those of us that use bikes to bring home gold and silver medals and placement on podiums. However, Cannondale’s Flying V is not designed to bring home gold, but rather, bacon and a carton of eggs on your way home from work. Whether or not you feel that carbon fiber has a place in the urban landscape isn’t of importance here because this is Cannondale we’re talking about, and they often set trends, rather than adapt to them, not to mention that the Flying V went on to win multiple awards for innovation and design in 2026, including the iF Design Award. Some folks live on bragging rights, and if you tell someone that you’re riding an e-bike valued at about the price of their used car and that it’s built out of carbon fiber, you may very well feel as though you’re looking down on the masses from a balcony of luxury and opulence. I mean, Cannondale was calling this one “the world’s first all-carbon fiber urban e-bike,” which is quite the bold statement considering that there have been other brands out there that gave the market a carbon fiber and urban-destined e-bike before 2025. While I can’t make out how Cannondale messed with compliance using this framework of tubes, one thing is obvious: the rear triangle of the bike is one that looks ripped right off of a gravel bike, with a dropped seat stay to create a bike of softness at the rear, even though the bike itself includes no suspension. The only real source of softness, aside from the flexion that carbon fiber provides, are a set of tires rolling in with 50c tube diameter, but the presence of fenders does mean that we can take them off and possibly choose slightly larger tires for a bit more squishiness and vibration-damping properties. Power is drawn from a 400 Wh CompactTube battery integrated into the down tube. Since it's not a removable one, that’s all the range we can tap into, but a range extender is also available for the model. According to sources, without the extender, around 70 miles (114 km) is the peak range, so quite the efficiency. An integrated battery pack also means taking your bike up a flight of stairs if you need to recharge, so you need to be able to handle around 40 lbs (18 kg) of e-bike on your shoulder. As for the rest of this seamless and rather eye-catching beast – I won’t lie, I'm kind of liking that whole framework that Cannondale has used to give the V its signature look – it’s completed with internal cable routing, lighting at the front and rear, a cargo rack for bringing home that bacon I talked about, and a backsweep handlebar, or the kind your granny grew up with, so aimed at the more laid-back urban rider. The question is: Does the Flying V belong in your life? Well, that’s for you to say, but what you can do is look for one at a local Cannondale dealer and take it out for a spin if possible. If you still don’t know what to do, then sleep on it. It seems like quite a few riders have since there’s only one review on the bike’s product page even though it's been on the market for nearly a year. Ride safe out there, wear a helmet. content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. On August 27, 2026, Judge Rita F. Lin of the Northern District of California ruled largely in favor of Anthropic PBC in its suit against the Department of War and other federal agencies over the government’s decision to bar all federal use of Anthropic’s AI products and prohibit defense contractors from doing business with the company. The case, Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War (No. 26-cv-01996-RFL), offers a rare judicial roadmap for how far the government can go when it decides a contractor is no longer “trustworthy”—and where that authority runs out. In February 2026, after Anthropic refused to drop contractual restrictions on using its Claude models for mass surveillance of Americans and lethal autonomous warfare, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and President Trump publicly directed every federal agency to stop using Anthropic’s technology and barred any defense contractor from doing business with Anthropic at all, even on matters unrelated to defense. The Department of War then formally designated Anthropic a “supply chain risk” under 10 U.S.C. § 3252, a statute designed to address sabotage by hostile foreign actors. The court declined to find the Presidential Directive itself constitutional as an ultra vires act and left standing the government’s basic right to choose its own AI vendor. The ruling does not require anyone to continue using Anthropic’s products. title: England v Pakistan: Tourists drop seven players, call up seven and release coach Sarfaraz Ahmed - BBC
content: Pakistan have not won a Test series in the UK for 30 years Pakistan have responded to their series defeat by England by taking the extraordinary step of dropping seven players, calling up five uncapped players and releasing their head coach. After two one-sided defeats in the first two Tests, the tourists have revamped their squad and backroom staff for the third and final match of the series at Edgbaston. Five of the players dropped - Muhammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman and Khurram Shahzad - have featured in the series so far, while Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Jafar have been sent home without playing. A total of seven players have been called up. Batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal have previous Test experience and join the quintet of uncapped newcomers. Spin-bowling all-rounder Arafat Minhas, left-arm seamer Mohammed Imran Jr, wicketkeeper Said Baig and all-rounders Mohammad Imran and Razaullah have all received call-ups. In addition, head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul have been released to be replaced by Pakistan white-ball coach Mike Hesson and former Australia seamer Ashley Noffke. The third Test in Birmingham begins on 9 September. Pakistan have been abject in the opening two Tests, losing the first at Headingley by an innings and the second at Lord's by 194 runs. They have been bowled out for less than 200 in each of their four innings. The response is remarkable. For a touring team to send home seven players and the head coach mid-series is unprecedented. Ex-Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja, also a former chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm trying to convince myself this is all OK, but it is not. "It just shows Pakistan cricket has hit a panic button. It's not good for the game, it's not good for the confidence of the players who have come in, or the for the players who are left, because it makes you a selfish team. "What is the guarantee they will get the results? Some of these guys have not played Test cricket. I've got no idea why this was done." Pakistan to meet King Charles after Lord's controversy Sarfaraz denies knowing about Pakistan threat to end tour Pakistan have a history of making eccentric decisions in the wake of defeats. On England's last tour of Pakistan in 2024, the hosts responded to losing the first Test, when England made a total in excess of 800, by playing the second Test on the same pitch in Multan. On that occasion, Pakistan used garden heaters and fans to dry the surface, to assist their spinners. The home side won the next two Tests to win the series 2-1. Now, among the seven players sent home are Salman, who captained in the first Test in the absence of the injured Babar Azam, then was dropped for the second. Also dropped is opener Imam-ul-Haq, who was criticised at Lord's for not attempting to bat in either innings after suffering a calf injury while fielding on the opening day. Raja, who played 57 Tests between 1984 and 1997, added: "I'm really not happy with the situation. "How many times have we seen this happen in world cricket? Never, ever. This is more like football, midway through the season, firing a manager. "If you ask me how things can be fixed, I've got no idea." The sweeping selection changes come after the Pakistan team were surrounded by controversy during the second Test. At lunch on the first day, the PCB threatened to cancel the remainder of the match and tour because of an interview with the sons of Imran Khan that was broadcast by Sky. Imran, the former Pakistan captain and prime minster, has been in prison for three years on charges of corruption, which he denies. Pakistan ultimately completed the Test, with both captain Babar and head coach Sarfaraz denying any knowledge of a planned boycott. title: King Harald V’s final journey revealed as Norway announces funeral plans - HOLA
content: Norway has announced the date of King Harald V’s funeral. The late monarch, who died on Friday, August 28, at the age of 89, will be laid to rest on Wednesday, September 9, following a service at Oslo Cathedral. The funeral will begin at 1 p.m. local time and will be led by Olav Fykse Tveit, presiding bishop of the Church of Norway. Oslo Bishop Sunniva Gylver will also participate, while cathedral organist Marcus André Berg and the Oslo Cathedral Choir will provide music. The ceremony will follow the Church of Norway’s traditional funeral liturgy. Oslo Cathedral previously hosted the funeral of Harald’s father, King Olav V, in January 1991. The day is expected to begin with a private ceremony at the Royal Palace attended by the monarch’s closest relatives. A ceremonial procession will then carry King Harald’s coffin from the palace along Karl Johans gate before turning onto Kirkegata and continuing toward Oslo Cathedral. Members of the Norwegian royal family will be joined by representatives of the country’s institutions, members of Norwegian society and international guests. Dedicated public and press areas will be established along the procession route as mourners gather in the capital. A 21-gun salute is also expected to be fired from Akershus Fortress in tribute to the late King. Following the funeral service, a smaller procession will accompany the coffin from Oslo Cathedral to Akershus Castle Church, where a private ceremony will be held. The gathering is expected to include the royal family, members of other European royal houses, foreign guests and a limited number of representatives from Norway’s official institutions. King Harald will ultimately be laid to rest in the Royal Mausoleum at Akershus Fortress, alongside members of his family, including his parents, King Olav V and Crown Princess Märtha, and his grandparents, King Haakon VII and Queen Maud. Following the burial, a double royal salute is reportedly set to be fired from the fortress. Flags across Norway, which have been flying at half-mast during the mourning period, will then be raised to full staff. Once the ceremonies at Akershus have concluded, the royal family and other attendees are expected to return to the Royal Palace in a procession of vehicles. King Haakon VIII and his family will then appear on the palace balcony to greet the people of Norway. A reception for members of the Norwegian government, relatives, foreign representatives and other funeral guests is expected to follow inside the palace. King Harald’s coffin was moved from the Red Salon to the Royal Chapel on Monday, August 31, in a solemn procession through the palace. The late King’s children and grandchildren carried the coffin, while Queen Sonja and Queen Mette-Marit followed behind. The crown, the Sword of State and several of Harald’s most important Norwegian and international orders were also included in the procession. The coffin was placed on a velvet-covered catafalque in the chapel and draped with the royal standard, surrounded by wreaths and floral tributes from the family. Members of the public will be able to file past the coffin and say a final goodbye beginning Tuesday, September 1, at 2 p.m. The Royal Chapel will remain open for public visits until 6 p.m. on September 8, the day before the funeral. King Harald died peacefully at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet at 6:35 a.m. on August 28. He had been hospitalized since August 17, initially receiving treatment related to anemia before his health deteriorated following a bacterial infection in his bloodstream. His coffin was transported to the Royal Palace later that day, accompanied by members of the royal family. Despite heavy rain, mourners lined parts of the route and later gathered outside the palace to leave flowers, candles and handwritten messages. Harald’s son immediately succeeded him as King Haakon VIII. In his first address as sovereign, the new King remembered his father as a warm and devoted family man and thanked Norwegians for mourning alongside the royal family. © ¡HOLA! title: Norway's Queen Mette-Marit joins procession to bring late King Harald V's coffin to royal chapel - Click2Houston
content: OSLO – The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title. Harald passed away Friday at age 89, and his son, the crown prince, immediately became King Haakon VIII. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Haakon, 53, will take the oath to Norway’s constitution on Tuesday. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. Mette-Marit has been largely absent from the public eye in the wake of her lung transplant in June. She was diagnosed in 2018 with pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive disease that damages and scars lung tissue. It can cause serious breathing problems, and there is no known cure. Mette-Marit and Queen Sonja, Harald’s widow, held hands and walked behind the coffin during Monday's procession. Since Harald’s death, the royal family and the country have been in an official state of mourning. Norwegians and visitors expressed their grief over the weekend by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. The coffin stayed in the palace’s Red Salon over the weekend before traveling to the royal chapel on Monday, where it will remain until the funeral. The public can go to the chapel to pay their respects to the late king beginning Tuesday, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. title: The “born free and equal” clauses and Lawrence v. Texas - SCOTUSblog
content: This is the third of seven introductory articles on the relevance for constitutional law of the “born free and equal” clauses, which appeared in the Declaration of Independence and in six out of 12 state constitutions when the federal Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791, and in 24 out of 37 state constitutions when the 14th Amendment was ratified in 1868. The “born free and equal” clause of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, for example, provided that: In my first two articles, I showed that the “born free and equal” idea is deeply rooted in American history and tradition as that phrase is used in such correctly decided cases as Washington v. Glucksberg (the right to assisted suicide is not deeply rooted in American history and tradition), McDonald v. City of Chicago (the Second Amendment’s right to own a handgun for self-protection extends to the states because it is deeply rooted in American history and tradition), and Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (the right to an abortion is not deeply rooted in American history and tradition). In this third introductory article, I want to examine the application of the “born free and equal” clauses to another famous “right to privacy” case: 2003’s Lawrence v. Texas, which struck down so-called “sodomy” laws banning oral and anal sex as unconstitutional. In my last article, I explained why: 1) there is no such thing as a constitutional “right to privacy” of the kind found incorrectly in Roe v. Wade, yet 2) why the outcome in Griswold v. Connecticut, the pivotal 1965 case striking down laws banning the use of contraceptives, is nonetheless correct under the privileges or immunities clause, which applied the “born and free and equal” clauses as modified by Corfield v. Coryell (discussed below) to the states. I’ll apply this analysis to Lawrence v. Texas to explain why I think that case was rightly decided but not for the reasons given by Justice Anthony Kennedy in his opinion for the court. To back up a bit, the seminal case of Corfield v. Coryell, decided in 1823, was dispositive as to the original meaning of the privileges or immunities clause of the 14th Amendment according to the framers of that amendment. In Corfield, Justice Bushrod Washington explained: Note that the language in italics makes clear that the 14th Amendment protects only rights deeply rooted in history and tradition. The language in bold face is a paraphrase of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780’s “born free and equal” clause and is a privilege or immunity of citizens of the United States. At the same time, the underlined passage critically limits the “born-free-and-equal” idea by making all rights “subject nevertheless to such restraints as the government may justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” This language marks the origin of what we today call the rational basis test (and what the Lochner-era Supreme Court wrongly called a reasonableness test). In Lawrence v. Texas, the Supreme Court struck down as unconstitutional a Texas sodomy law that applied only to gay and lesbian couples. The court said in dicta that sodomy laws applying to heterosexual couples also violated the Constitution. It did so based on the so-called “right to privacy” found in Griswold v. Connecticut. Since I argued in my last article that there is no such right, I turn now to whether the decision in Lawrence v. Texas was correct under the “born free and equal” clauses and the privileges or immunities clause of the 14th Amendment as discussed above and in my two prior articles. The first question is whether a right to commit so-called “sodomy,” either by heterosexual or gay and lesbian couples, is deeply rooted in our nation’s history and tradition; that is, whether this is part of the “born-free-and-equal” idea that everyone has the right “to enjoy life and liberty” and to “pursue and obtain happiness and safety.” While the right to commit sodomy has long been criminalized, freedom among committed adult couples to enjoy sexual relationships in every way is arguably covered by the deeply rooted rights to “enjoy liberty” and to “pursue and obtain happiness and safety.” This question then becomes what is the correct level of generality at which to analyze this issue. Sodomy laws, while of ancient vintage, have almost never been enforced in modern times, except against gay and lesbian people. Although all 50 states and the District of Columbia had such laws in 1960, by 2003, when Lawrence v. Texas was decided, 37 out of the 50 states had repealed their sodomy laws, and these laws were almost never enforced by the 13 states which retained them in 2003. Indeed, the only way to get prosecuted for sodomy in 2003 in the 13 states that retained such laws was to call the police to come to your house during the commission of such an act (which is exactly what happened in Lawrence). Under these circumstances, one must remember Judge Robert H. Bork’s prophetic words in “The Tempting of America: The Political Seduction of the Law,” in which Bork, one of the founding fathers of modern originalism, stated that: “The world changes in which unchanging values [I would say ‘legal texts’] find their application.” This is a profound observation for an originalist. It means that originalists must not only look at the original public meaning of a text when it is adopted: they must also apply that text to a modern world which presents new technologies and changed circumstances such that the constitutional text must be translated to apply to them. Translation occurs, for example, when we apply the First Amendment’s protection of freedom of speech and of the press to expressive conduct like flag burning, or to hand-written material in a private diary, or in a private letter to a friend, or in broadcast movies, radio, television, and the internet where freedom of expression is constitutionally protected even in the absence of speech – a vocal utterance – or in the absence of a “printing” press. In “The Tempting of America,” Bork had no trouble finding that the 14th Amendment’s overarching commitment to racial equality, relied upon in Brown v. Board of Education, trumped the original expected application of many of the 14th Amendment’s framers who mistakenly said in congressional debates, in 1868, that racial equality was somehow consistent with segregated public schools and anti-miscegenation laws. This was clearly not true by 1954, as to public schools, and by 1967, as to anti-miscegenation laws.The Supreme Court was therefore right to hold that public school segregation and anti-miscegenation laws are unconstitutional in the modern world even though many of the members of Congress who voted for the 14th Amendment said otherwise. Exactly the same thing holds true with respect to sodomy laws in 2003. In 1868, the framers of the 14th Amendment, when they wrote Corfield v. Coryell’s version of the “born free and equal” right (subject to a rational basis test) into the privileges or immunities clause of the 14th Amendment, mistakenly thought that sodomy laws were somehow consistent with the “born-free-and-equal” idea. As late as 1986’s Bowers v. Hardwick, a 5-4 majority of the Supreme Court agreed. But by 2003, with only 13 states having sodomy laws on the books, which they almost never enforced, and decades after the birth control pill was legalized on May 9, 1960, which helped launch a sexual revolution, the rise of the modern feminist movement, and the gay rights movement, it became as difficult to square sodomy laws with the “born-free-and-equal” command of the privileges or immunities clause as it was to square segregated public schools and laws banning inter-racial marriage with the “no race discrimination” command of the 14th Amendment. Thus, when Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954, or when Loving v. Virginia was decided in 1967, or when Lawrence v. Texas was decided in 2003, it was not enough to rely on original expected applications of the framers of the 14th Amendment, which, in fact, undercut the 14th Amendment’s central textual rights. In other words, an originalist judge cannot let constitutional rights – even open-ended rights – be overridden by a clearly mistaken, original expected application of the relevant text. This still leaves open the key question of whether sodomy laws should have been upheld in 2003 under the rational basis test. As noted earlier, that test also originates in Justice Washington’s Corfield v. Coryell opinion, which states that the rights to “enjoy liberty” and to “pursue and obtain happiness and safety” are “subject nevertheless to such restraints as the government may justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” Were sodomy laws in 2003, or today in 2026, then “justly prescribed for the general good of the whole [people]”? The answer is “no” for the reasons given by Justice Byron White in his concurrence in Griswold v. Connecticut. There is a lack of means-ends fit to sodomy laws: they intrude on a highly personal sexual liberty right for the dubious purpose of promoting only sex that could lead to childbirth. Yet in a world where contraceptive use is almost universal (even among Catholics, whose church still formally prohibits it), isolating out the act of sodomy for punishment makes little sense. One could just as plausibly punish non-procreative sex by couples using birth control, by heterosexual couples where the woman is post-menopausal, or even masturbation, by individual men and women. All these activities are sexual acts that do not lead to the possibility of childbirth. Is there any rational basis for criminalizing sodomy but not such other conduct? The answer is “no.” Punishing the non-procreative sexual acts of gays and lesbians is especially unfair to such persons given they have no control over who they are attracted to. As my friend Akhil Reed Amar has argued many times on this site, the citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment, along with the “born free and equal” clauses, commands birthright equality, regardless of whether one is born gay or straight. For this reason, the 13 mostly unenforced state sodomy laws on the books flunk the rational basis test. While I think Lawrence v. Texas thus reached the right outcome in holding sodomy laws to be irrational and unconstitutional, I believe Justice Anthony Kennedy’s majority opinion is vacuous, for many of the reasons pointed out by Justice Antonin Scalia in his dissent. As Scalia made clear, Kennedy’s majority opinion appears to write John Stuart Mills’ harm principal from “On Liberty” (that one’s actions should only by limited so much as they do harm to others) into the 14th Amendment, which is just as wrong as writing Herbert Spencer’s “Social Statics” into that amendment as the court did in the infamous case of Lochner v. New York striking down as unconstitutional perfectly valid laws establishing maximum working hours. To be clear: Among the many laws that I think rationally trump an individual’s right to “enjoy liberty” and “pursue and obtain happiness and safety” are laws criminalizing: 1) polyamory, 2) prostitution, 3) incest, 4) suicide, and 5) the use of dangerous drugs and narcotics regulated by the government. As Scalia once told me, and as I entirely agree, the people who are disproportionately “harmed” by all six of the activities listed above are women, children, and the elderly who are among the most vulnerable members of society. Laws banning these six activities, and probably many others, are then subject “to such restraints as the government may justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” The six criminal laws listed above easily pass the rational basis test, unlike laws against sodomy but which ban no other forms of non-procreative sex. Americans, and the Constitution, have always opted for a regime of “ordered liberty” and not for constitutionalizing John Stuart Mill’s harm test. In my next column, I will analyze through the lens of the “born free and equal” clause the Supreme Court’s gay and lesbian marriage opinion in Obergefell v. Hodges, in which it found a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law. title: Track by Track: V Torres – Woman - The Indy Review
content:
LA-based singer/songwriter V Torres captivated me with the first three singles from her upcoming album Woman. The title track, “Winter Solstice” and “That Night” showcased her vibrant and roots mix of indie rock and Americana. Torres describes her new album as “a journey” and a “testament on things that have shaped the woman I am today.” With the album dropping tomorrow, September 1st, Torres gave us a track-by-track breakdown of every song on the album, which you can read below! The idea behind beginnings started with the concept that every ending leads to a new beginning and every beginning will have an ending. It’s the cycle of life. The thought that everything is temporary. Something that has become somewhat of a mantra for me. It also focuses on how hard it is when you feel ready to love someone, but they are not ready to receive that love. It’s that tender moment of realizing that everyone’s timing is different and their own. The song encourages evolving and strengthening the relationship with yourself, as that is the one that needs to be looked at before you can look at relationships with others. How can we change if we always stay the same? When writing this song, I went through iterations of how the rhythm of the guitar would end up before settling on the staccato beat of the track. I think it lends itself to an interesting way for the vocal melody to dance around the guitars in the verses. I also wanted to add an 808 to the beginning of the bridge so that the listener could really feel the shift and the weight of the song opening up. I really love how the bridge builds into the breakdown chorus. Fun fact about this song is that it was not originally slated for the record. I sent my co-producer my demo of it and he insisted that it belonged on the record. I am so glad we included it. This is the title track of the record. “Woman” is my song for Women that really steps into the journey of being a Woman and being inspired by Women. The constant grind women experience, and often-times, the attending to the needs of others, while trying to keep it all together.  The grief we experience in letting go of the past versions of ourselves and the roles we play: lover, mother, caretaker, friend, etc. There is still a hopefulness somewhere in the journey and strength and acceptance of life and the work we have to do to heal. The light we see in this is the letting our guard down and being open again to love. When I first wrote the song, I wanted the acoustic guitar and drums to drive the rhythm of the song. It feels as though you are riding horseback through the desert. My lead guitarist, Kira Lingman, added her lead lines to bring a Latin/americana feeling to the track. Making the music video for Woman was really fun. Cinematographer, Dylan Pelle, approached me and said he wanted to make a desert themed music video and that he thought my music would lend well to it. We listened to all the songs on the record, and it was clear that Woman was the track to use. It already has a cinematic feeling to it, and we wanted to capture that old spaghetti western vibe. We shot in the Joshua Tree desert, at an old grimy motel in Rosemond, and at an abandoned music venue in Hermosa Beach. It was a lot of fun to see our vision come to life. This is a track I wrote when a very close friend of mine had lost her brother to a tragic accident. I was in a position of wanting to console and be there for them but there really was nothing I could do for them at the time. These words came out fast and the song was written on the Winter Solstice, hence the name. This friend is one of those people who makes everyone feel loved and good. They are always the one making everyone laugh. They had been there for me through really hard times, and this song was written for them during this time. Sometimes you don’t have the words to express what you want to say. Sometimes the act of just giving someone a silent hug is enough. I wanted this song to embody that feeling of being there for someone who’s always there for everyone else and I think in some part of this it was also giving myself that love. Knowing that you can love someone from afar and you can love yourself and hold yourself up even when you’re feeling alone. Visually, the Winter Solstice is the darkest night of the year, but it also leads to more light coming through in the near future. I felt like the visual of that dark night was present in this song but the sliver of light on the horizon was a sign of hope and something to look forward to as well. Sonically, I heard the harmonies of the chorus in my head when I was writing the song. I wanted it to start a little more rocking and surf/punk like but then turn into this beautiful choir during the chorus lines. I also wanted a slide guitar in the song to give it a little bit more americana and that tinge of country. When I hear the slide guitar, it feels like a hug, it feels like comfort and can bring me to tears, which is exactly what this song is really all about to me. This song is about the possibilities of a new adventure and allowing yourself to be open to vulnerability. It paints a picture of the moment when you go from being friends with someone to falling for them and seeing them in a completely different way. It’s highlighting that scary and exciting part of letting your guard down. The song sits in the anticipation of letting go and letting them know how you feel. Lingering in that moment when there isn’t an answer yet can be exciting to think of the potential that life has ahead for you. Sonically, I wanted those intro harmonies to shine and cut through. I really love how the song is a little more stripped down during the verses and a little more dance-y than the rest of the tracks. The guitar line I play after the first verse was inspired by the sound of the Breeders and it’s one of my favorite parts of the song along with the vocal intensity of chorus that comes after the bridge. The ending speaking part in the song is my grandmother speaking the bridge line in Spanish. I wanted her to be a part of this record and had her send me a voice note to include in the song. True story, I went to Joshua Tree for the first time and stayed in an air bnb on a property that got raided by the police in search of the body of a woman who had gone missing weeks prior. Yes, it’s crazy and yes, it happened. This moment was scary and tragic, and it got me thinking about how finite life is. I started thinking about my own life and that I wasn’t living my most authentic self. It got me thinking about what is “right” and what is “wrong” and what is the grey area in life. Can we live in that area? Being raised catholic was a lot of things but the whole “sinning” part of life and not being able to express your true self without it being thought of as unconventional or just plain wrong was running through my head. This song explores a desert landscape where there is no right or wrong, just the grey. I love how this song is more of a harder rock song than the rest of the record. I added a harmony in the chorus that I feel brings a little psychedelic rock into the song. I really love the bridge of the song that takes the song on a segue into a really cool, stripped-down groove. My lead guitarist, Kira Lingman, wrote that bridge line on the guitar and we really ran with it from a production standpoint to create this interesting breakdown which includes me using the WAH pedal for the first time on a record. The production feeling on the bridge makes me feel like something BECK would have done. This is probably the oldest song I wrote for this record. I was going through my divorce about 9 years ago. My ex called me and asked if I knew what today was. Thinking, thinking, I had no idea what he was talking about. He said it was six months to the day since we split. I had heard someone earlier in one of my yoga classes say that time was just a man-made thing. That thought came right back up to me when I realized I was not tracking this time period like he was. I immediately started writing Great Escape. The song is about leaving a situation that is not right for you anymore. It is both the knowing what you did was the right thing but also the challenges with loneliness in the aftermath. You need someone to console you and tell you everything will be okay, but you do not have that person to do so. When I wrote the song, I really wanted it to have variations in timing and melodies. I knew that I wanted the song to start with a faster tempo that felt driving and I wanted the chorus to be in half time. I felt like the half time chorus really spoke to the message of the song and symbolized the feeling of time and processing the emotion of the track. Conversely, I wanted the bridge of the song to feel like you were running through the middle of the night frantically searching for some kind of sign that you are going to be okay. I wanted it to feel chaotic and uncontrolled. The BPM of the song changes from 119 to 151. If you listen to the beginning of the song right after the end of the song, it seems SO slow, but it works in context of the song from start to finish. It was challenging recording the song and understanding where it sat the best tempo-wise. At one point I suggested a slower tempo from the offset, and it was exactly what the track needed to really get to the right place. It’s sludgy, beautiful and electric how it all turned out. I feel like it’s the most epic song on the record. This song is about getting older and knowing less. Realizing that so many thoughts and influences go into your decisions as a younger person and the older you become, the more you realize that you really don’t need to think that hard.  It is also about opening up myself to loving again after patterns of running away. Sonically, I had a demo of this track that I gave to my co-producer, and it was really bare boned with just guitar and vocals. We almost wanted to keep the demo version because there was something really beautiful and vulnerable that was perfect about it. We opted into re-recording it through amp splitting with a ‘72 Princeton reverb and a Roland jazz chorus. I was really pleased with how the guitar tones and vocals shine through on this short and sweet track. Pre-Save the album here (or starting tomorrow, play it wherever you stream music).
